Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a school join all its laptops into one network?Show the answer

So people can communicate, and share things such as files and one printer.

Recap of 6.3.1. Look at the cables in the picture.

items.prompt: Can Ana print on the Printer?
items.explain: Ana → Switch → Printer. Both are plugged into the switch, so the data gets there.

items.prompt: Can Chi send Ben a message?
items.explain: Chi has no cable. Chi is not joined to the switch, so nothing can travel from Chi.

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: following the cables

steps.text: A similar network. Mai and Tom are plugged into a switch. The Printer is plugged in too. Sam is on the table with no cable.
steps.visual: Mai, Tom, Printer: cables to the switch. Sam: no cable.

The switch passes the data on. Is the Printer plugged into the switch too? Yes, so the data gets there.
Can Sam send Tom a message? Start at Sam. There is no cable to follow, so the message cannot leave.

steps.content:
Do Now: Count the Cables (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does each device need a cable of its own to the switch?Show the answer

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: counting cables

steps.text: A similar question. 4 laptops and 2 printers are each plugged into one switch. How many cables?
Each device has one socket, so each device has one cable, going to the switch.
Count the devices: 4 laptops and 2 printers.
Two rooms. Room A and Room B each have a switch. A switch has many sockets, so one switch can plug into the other.
Now do the Do Now: count the devices for part a. For part b, think how few cables join the two switches.

steps.label: Joining Networks Together
steps.content:
6.3 Computer Networks

Joining Networks Together

Year 6

  • Today: how two networks can be joined.
  • How data travels a long way, all round the world.
  • Join networks in the 3D lab, then send data across them.
Think → Pair → ShareYour home has a network. Your school has a network. Predict: can a laptop at home send a message to a laptop at school? What would it need?Show the answer

Only if something joins the two networks, so the message can pass from one to the other.

steps.label: Joining Two Networks
steps.content:
Joining Two Networks

Think → Pair → ShareHome and school each have a network with a switch. Nothing joins the two networks. Predict: can Ana at home send Chi at school a message? Why?Show the answer

No. Nothing joins the two networks, so the message has no way to get from home to school.

  • A switch joins the devices inside one network.
  • A router joins two or more networks together.
  • Data from Ana goes to her switch, then to the router.
  • The router sends it on to the school network, where Chi receives it.

steps.label: Predict: Switch or Router?
steps.content:
Predict: Switch or Router?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is it not enough for the home network and the school network to be close to each other?Show the answer

Being close does not join them. Data can only travel along a cable or Wi-Fi.

items.prompt: Which joins the laptops inside one classroom?
items.explain: A switch joins the devices inside one network.

items.prompt: Which joins the home network to the school network?
items.explain: A router joins different networks and passes data between them.

items.prompt: The cable from the router to the school switch comes out. Can Ana still send Chi a message?
items.explain: The router is no longer joined to the school network, so the message cannot get there.

steps.label: What Is the Internet?
steps.content:
What Is the Internet?

Think → Pair → ShareThere are millions of networks in homes, schools and shops. Predict: how could a laptop in Bangkok send a message to a laptop in London?Show the answer

The networks are joined to each other by routers. The message passes from router to router until it reaches London.

  • The internet is many networks that are joined to each other.
  • Every home, school and shop network has a router.
  • The routers are joined to other routers, all round the world.
  • So a message can travel from any network to any other network.

steps.label: Router to Router
steps.content:
Router to Router

Think → Pair → ShareLook at the picture. No cable goes straight from Ana to Ben. Predict: how does Ana's message still get to Ben?Show the answer

Each router passes the message on to the next one, one step closer to Ben, until it arrives.

  • The path data takes from one device to another is its route.
  • Each router receives the data, then sends it on to the next router.
  • No one cable goes all round the world. So data travels a long way one step at a time.

steps.label: Predict: Follow the Route
steps.content:
Predict: Follow the Route

Think → Pair → ShareWhy might a message to a faraway country pass through many routers?Show the answer

No single cable goes that far. Each router passes it on towards where it is going.

Look at the route from Ana to Ben.

items.prompt: How many routers does the message pass through, from Ana to Ben?
items.explain: Home router, Router A, Router B, Router C, School router: 5 routers. Ana and Ben are laptops, not routers.

items.prompt: The cable between Router B and Router C breaks. There is no other route. Can Ana send Ben a message?
items.explain: The only route is broken in the middle, so the message cannot get past Router B.

steps.label: Activity 1: Join Networks with Routers
steps.content:
Activity 1: Join Networks with Routers

Think → Pair → ShareWhy try to send a message before you add the router?Show the answer

You see it fail. Then you know it is the router that makes it work.

Do the missions on the right in order: Join Two Networks, The Internet, then Hop by Hop. Predict before you send. Walk with W A S D.

steps.label: Data in Packets
steps.content:
Data in Packets

Think → Pair → ShareA big photo has to cross the internet. Predict: is it better to send it in one big piece, or in lots of small parts? Why?Show the answer

Lots of small parts. If one small part gets lost, only that part is sent again. And many people can share the same cables, taking turns.

  • Data is split into small parts called packets.
  • Routers send and receive data as packets. Each packet travels on its own.
  • At the end, the packets are put back together.
  • If one packet is lost, only that one is sent again.

steps.label: Why Number the Packets?
steps.content:
Why Number the Packets?

Think → Pair → SharePackets can take different routes, and some routes are slower. Predict: what could go wrong when the packets arrive?Show the answer

They could arrive in the wrong order, so the message or photo would be mixed up.

  • Each packet has a number.
  • Packets can take different routes, so they can arrive in a different order.
  • The computer at the end sorts the packets by their numbers.
  • If a link breaks, routers send the packets another way, if there is one.

steps.label: Predict: Put It Back Together
steps.content:
Predict: Put It Back Together

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is it good to split a photo into many small packets, and not send it in one piece?Show the answer

A small packet is quick to send again if it gets lost, and many people can share the cables, taking turns.

items.prompt: These packets arrive: 3 "the", 1 "Please", 4 "door", 2 "open". What is the message?
items.explain: Sort by number: 1 Please, 2 open, 3 the, 4 door.

items.prompt: Why does each packet have a number?
options: So the packets can be put back in the right order
So the cable knows which laptop to go to
items.explain: Packets can arrive in a different order. Their numbers tell the computer which order to put them back in.

items.prompt: One link on the route breaks, but there is another route. What happens to the packets?
options: They wait until the link is mended
items.explain: Routers send the packets another way, if there is one.

steps.label: Activity 2: Send Packets
steps.content:
Activity 2: Send Packets

Think → Pair → ShareWhy watch where each packet goes, and not only whether it arrives?Show the answer

You can see the packets take different routes and arrive in a different order.

Do the missions on the right in order: Messages in Packets, Different Paths, Find Another Way, then the Connect the Town challenge (no help).

steps.label: Check: Count Them
steps.content:

Think → Pair → ShareHow can the computer at the end tell that a packet has not arrived?Show the answer

The numbers have a gap: a number is not there.

Type a number for each.

Total: 2 marks
